teamknitt: Configuring, Observing and Intervening
in LLM-Agent Teams through the Lens of
Dynamical-Systems and Human-Team Theory

Goran Mitevski Email: rolevski.mk@icloud.com
November 2026
Abstract

Most frameworks for teams of large language model (LLM) agents fix the team’s shape inside the software: who talks to whom, how much is passed along, and what a human can do once a run has started. Human-team research has spent six decades asking exactly those questions, with competing answers about where team phenomena live (in the members or in their interaction), how team-level properties arise (by aggregation or by differentiation), and what distinguishes what a team does from how a team is. I propose using that body of theory as the organizing lens for configuring, observing and intervening in LLM-agent teams, without assuming that its findings transfer.

I introduce teamknitt, a framework and open reference implementation in which a user configures a team of 1–16 AI agents for task completion, solution generation, achieving a goal or a research mission; selects one of fourteen deterministic routing topologies or a custom directed graph; chooses a sharing profile that limits what may travel along permitted routes; and binds complementary sources, external representations, work dependencies, version-specific handoffs and an expertise directory. The same recorded process can then be observed through two groups of views: non-system views that locate explanation in member reports and behavior, and system views that locate it in distributed problem-solving, differentiated transactive memory, interactive coordination and team dynamics. Interventions are explicit and human-led: reviewed reconfiguration between runs, planned disturbances before a run, and private feedback, pause, resume or stop applied at dependency-wave boundaries during a run. Every record keeps “queued”, “applied”, “context assembled”, “understood” and “improved” as separate claims. Emergent states such as trust, cohesion and shared understanding are declared unmeasured.

This is an idea and system-description paper. The contribution is a configuration space, a reference implementation and a set of falsifiable hypotheses about topology, information flow and intervention timing in LLM-agent teams. A planned line of study extends the author’s earlier work on the dynamics of distributed software teams: whether the fractal scaling and flexibility of the communication output exchanged between members—and between members running on different models—is associated with better task and team performance. No comparative result is reported, and no topology is claimed to be best.

1  Introduction

A team of LLM agents has an organization whether or not anyone chose it. A chain of specialists, a hub that collects proposals, a round of debate among peers and a fully connected chat each decide who sees what and when. The choice is usually buried in the architecture of the orchestration framework [24, 17, 35, 43], or delegated to an optimizer that searches over communication graphs against a benchmark signal [47, 46, 18]. Both approaches answer the organizational question before the work starts and give the user little to inspect or adjust once it has.

Human-team research has a long, unfinished argument about the same question. One tradition treats the team as the context in which individual attributes add up: the input–process–output (IPO) framework [28, 14] and the compositional reading of team-level constructs [22]. A second tradition moves to the system level while keeping psychological constructs—emergent states such as shared mental models, trust and psychological safety that develop over repeated episodes [26, 20, 9]. A third treats team cognition as something a team does in interaction rather than something it has [6, 11], and reads variability in coordination as a source of adaptability rather than noise. Gorman and colleagues [11] summarize the divide as non-system versus system explanations: whether a team phenomenon is located in the members or in the interaction process.

The present paper takes these distinctions seriously as design questions for LLM-agent teams, while refusing the shortcut of assuming that human findings carry over. If the organization of an agent team changes what it produces, a user should be able to choose the organization explicitly, observe the work through more than one explanatory lens, and intervene in ways whose scope is recorded. teamknitt is a concrete attempt to make that possible. It is a follow-up to Labtune [32], which treated laboratory organization and information sharing as controlled variables for LLM-agent research, and to the author’s thesis work on the dynamics of distributed software teams’ creative processes [31]. Where Labtune offered six editable laboratory designs for research missions, teamknitt generalizes the mission to tasks, brainstorming and goals, replaces lab designs with fourteen routing topologies over 1–16 members, binds the team’s problem-solving structure explicitly, and adds research-informed views and human-led intervention. It ships its own runtime and makes no automated organizational improvement.

The paper has five commitments:

  • •

    Configuration before execution. Purpose, members, routing, sharing, bindings, models, tools and finite budgets are explicit and user-selected. Topology filters exposure; it grants no decision authority and creates no capacity (Section 4).

  • •

    Two explanatory lenses on one record. Non-system and system views project the same configuration and trace. Switching views never changes the team (Section 5).

  • •

    Three distinctions kept apart. Explanatory locus (non-system/system), form of emergence (compositional/compilational) and process/state/outcome are related but separate axes, and the implementation does not collapse them (Section 2).

  • •

    Explicit, bounded intervention. Reviewed reconfiguration, planned disturbances and boundary-applied feedback, pause, resume and stop, with queued, applied, assembled, understood and improved recorded as distinct claims (Section 6).

  • •

    Declared non-measurement. Trust, cohesion, psychological safety, efficacy, potency, shared understanding, emergence, synchrony and attractors are not inferred from software traces. What is recorded is operational; what is not measured is named.

Scope of this paper

This is an exploratory preprint and system description. I contribute (i) the framing of team topology, information flow and intervention as explicit, theory-indexed variables for LLM-agent teams; (ii) a formal configuration space and the design principles that constrain it; (iii) an open reference implementation [33] with offline demonstrations, grouped views and an intervention queue; and (iv) falsifiable hypotheses and a protocol for testing them (Section 8). I report no comparative result. A persona label assigns a reasoning role; it is not evidence of expertise, and completion of a workflow is not evidence that the user’s goal was achieved.

2  Background and related work

2.1  Three distinctions from human-team research

Explanatory locus

Non-system explanations locate a team phenomenon in member attributes, knowledge and skills, or in their aggregate; system explanations locate it in the interaction process, which has properties no member possesses alone [11]. This is an orientation, not a quality ranking, and system is not a synonym for complexity science: conventional IPO and IMOI models also include interaction, feedback and contingencies [20].

Form of emergence

Kozlowski and Klein [22] distinguish compositional emergence, where a team-level construct is isomorphic with its member-level counterpart and can be formed by means, sums or agreement, from compilational emergence, where the team-level pattern is a differentiated configuration with no simple individual analogue. Shared mental models measured as within-team agreement [3, 27, 7] are the textbook compositional case; transactive memory—knowing who knows what, with differentiated encoding and retrieval [42, 23]—is compilational. The distinction is related to explanatory locus but not identical to it.

Process, state and outcome

Marks, Mathieu and Zaccaro [26] separate what teams do (transition and action processes, with interpersonal processes spanning both) from emergent states that describe how teams are, and organize processes temporally across recurring episodes. Outcomes feed later inputs [20]. The distinction matters for software: a publication, an exposure or an acknowledgement is an operational process record. It is not cohesion [1], trust, psychological safety [9] or shared understanding.

Distributed, interactive and dynamical accounts

Distributed cognition [19] and its extension to teams [29] widen the unit of analysis to people, artifacts, tools and representation transformations. Interactive team cognition [6] treats cognition as situated interaction activity. Coordination dynamics [21, 40] and the dynamical-systems view of teams [11] supply principles—local–global stability, substrate independence, cross-level effects—and interventions such as perturbation training [10], alongside meta-analytic evidence on team training [37]. Complex adaptive systems are a wider tradition [16, 30]; citing them motivates questions, not conclusions.

2.2  Distributed teams and creative dynamics

The dynamical view also motivated the author’s earlier empirical work on distributed software teams [31]. Using GitHub records of one organization, that study applied detrended fluctuation analysis to code-addition time series and estimated maximal Lyapunov exponents of daily discussion density, following Guastello’s treatment of creative discussion groups [13]. Long-range correlation was present in the development dynamics, and the discussion that accompanied the more stable software product was more flexible in the quantitative sense used there. The thesis also noted that such measurements could inform when, and how much, an artificial teammate should intervene in a creative process. teamknitt follows up on that interest from the other side: it records the team process at the granularity of dependency waves and makes the intervention decision explicit and human-led. It does not estimate those exponents. Wave records are short and unevenly spaced; the estimators belong in a research agenda (Section 8), not in a product dashboard. The agenda carries the question forward in a form the earlier data could not support: because every contribution, exposure and acknowledgement in a teamknitt run is timestamped and attributed, the communication output between members—its volume, its timing and its lexical content—can be assembled into series long enough to ask whether its scaling properties relate to how well the team did, and whether that relation changes when members run on different models.

2.3  LLM-agent systems

Table 1 places teamknitt among LLM-based approaches that touch the organizational question. Reasoning methods such as Tree and Graph of Thoughts [45, 2] structure intermediate thoughts within an agent; teamknitt is agnostic about them and organizes agents. Research systems—Agent Laboratory [39], the AI co-scientist [12], the AI Scientist [25], the Virtual Lab [41]—fix a division of labour and an exchange pattern; AgentRxiv [38] adds cross-lab sharing of reports. MacNet [36], GPTSwarm [47] and G-Designer [46] study or optimize communication topology; IMACS [5] routes tasks to protocols with a bandit; AutoGen [43] is general orchestration infrastructure. Failure analyses [4], evidence that teams can hold experts back [34], and evidence that generative tools raise individual output while reducing collective diversity [8] all suggest that more communication is not automatically better collaboration. The Collaborative Intelligence benchmark [44] evaluates an agent as a teammate on eight capabilities after conditioning on solo competence; teamknitt treats that as a member-focused (non-system) view and keeps probe evidence in a separate context.

Relation to Labtune

Labtune [32] asked which laboratory organization, under which communication policy, suits which research problem, and supplied the apparatus for asking it. teamknitt is based on Labtune and keeps its conservative core: budgets are conserved under delegation, information crosses boundaries only through controller-published views at phase barriers, and the system never redesigns its own organization. It departs in four ways. The mission generalizes from research to any task, brainstorming prompt or goal. The organizational variable changes from six prose-defined lab designs to fourteen deterministic routing presets plus custom directed links, with explicit bindings of sources, representations, work and handoffs. The observation layer is grouped by explanatory locus rather than by research phase. And intervention becomes a first-class, bounded operation. Bayesian analysis and model-assisted priors are not carried over; descriptive records and frequentist count and interval analysis remain where applicable.

3  Design principles

The implementation follows eight rules. They are conservative on purpose: the aim is to make organizational differences observable, not to make a team appear autonomous or effective.

  1. P1.

    The user configures the team. Purpose, member count, roles, topology, sharing, models, tools, delegation and budgets are explicit. Drafts write nothing; applying a draft is a separate reviewed step with a private backup, blocked by the run lock. Larger teams never raise budgets.

  2. P2.

    Topology filters exposure and nothing else. Routes decide which peer views and generated notes a member may encounter. A hub routes information; it acquires no veto. A hierarchy is a tree of routes, not a chain of command. Directed routes imply no reply.

  3. P3.

    Sharing is a policy applied at barriers. Publications validate before a wave commits; unfinished same-wave output is never exposed. A read budget bounds cross-member exposure per episode, including generated notes.

  4. P4.

    Exposure is not noninterference. A later contribution can relay what a member encountered along any later permitted route. Changing a route does not erase previous exposure; the record keeps the history.

  5. P5.

    Access, exposure, noticing, publication, citation and acknowledgement are distinct. An acknowledgement confirms that a specific version was encountered; it does not imply agreement, understanding or correctness.

  6. P6.

    Views never change the team. Non-system and system views, snapshots and the live monitor are presentation-only; they make no model calls and cannot write configuration.

  7. P7.

    Interventions are explicit, private and bounded. Requests are drafts until applied, bind one run and configuration, and are acknowledged at the next dependency-wave boundary. Feedback is task context, never a permission or budget grant.

  8. P8.

    Nothing is inferred that is not measured. Emergent psychological states, emergence itself, attractors, synchrony and causal intervention effects are not estimated from execution logs. Completion is not goal achievement.

4  The teamknitt model

Figure 1 shows the four steps the user moves through and the records that govern each step. The user configures a team, sets the task, observes the work through chosen views, and intervenes within recorded scope. The engine compiles the configuration into a task-team workflow of dependency waves, schedules bounded member frames, publishes permitted views at barriers, and retains contributions for human review.

4.1  Configuration space

A team configuration is a tuple

𝒯=(p,N,G,π,Σ,Δ,ℳ,ℬ,𝒟),\mathcal{T}=(p,\;N,\;G,\;\pi,\;\Sigma,\;\Delta,\;\mathcal{M},\;\mathcal{B},\;\mathcal{D}), (1)

where pp is the purpose, one of task, brainstorm, goal or research; N∈{1,…,16}N\in\{1,\dots,16\} the member count; G=(V,E)G=(V,E) a directed routing graph over members V={1,…,N}V=\{1,\dots,N\} drawn from a preset or given as custom links (Section 4.2); π=(ℓ,w,W)\pi=(\ell,w,W) the sharing policy, with profile ℓ\ell one of none, low, intermediate, high or wisdom_only, wisdom flag ww and read budget WW in words (Section 4.3); Σ\Sigma the problem-solving bindings (Section 4.4); Δ\Delta the delegation limits; ℳ\mathcal{M} the provider, model and tool bindings; ℬ\mathcal{B} the finite budgets (requests, wall time, concurrency); and 𝒟\mathcal{D} an optional set of planned disturbances (Section 6). The configuration is loaded from strict YAML, validated, and hashed into an identity stored with every plan, run and snapshot. Initialization, drafting, planning, viewing and demonstration make no provider calls, so the configuration space can be explored for free.

4.2  Routing topologies

Fourteen presets define EE deterministically for any N≤16N\leq 16 (Table 2; Figure 2). Reciprocal presets add both directions of a link; directed presets add one. A single member has no peer links, and small layouts can coincide (a two-member ring is a chain). Custom links are exactly the listed directed pairs; an empty list isolates every member. Presets are routing definitions, not inferred optimal organizations. Two consequences follow from P2 and P4. First, member 1 in a hub, wheel, broadcast or gather layout is a routing position, not a leader: it cannot veto, rank or create resources. Second, a diagram line denotes a permitted route, not causal influence; with sufficient waves, content can relay across a chain or around a ring, and the record will show where it did.

4.3  Sharing profiles and exposure

Sharing limits how much, and what kind of, content can travel along permitted routes (Table 3). Let oi​(t)o_{i}(t) denote member ii’s published representations at barrier tt, and VπV_{\pi} the controller’s filter for profile π\pi. Member jj’s context evolves as

Cj​(t+1)=Cj​(t)∪truncW⁡(Vπ​({oi​(t):(i→j)∈E})),C_{j}(t+1)\;=\;C_{j}(t)\,\cup\,\operatorname{trunc}_{W}\!\Big(V_{\pi}\big(\{\,o_{i}(t):(i\to j)\in E\,\}\big)\Big), (2)

where truncW\operatorname{trunc}_{W} bounds the combined exposure, including generated notes, to WW words per episode. Notes are not an extra channel: they obey the same routes and the same budget. User-supplied sources have their own reader grants and are not subject to EE. Shared writable workspaces require high. All publications in a wave validate before the wave commits, so a member never sees a peer’s unfinished same-wave output. The equation describes a filter on exposure, not a guarantee of noninterference (P4): what jj encounters at tt may reappear, transformed, in oj​(t+1)o_{j}(t+1) and travel further along (j→k)∈E(j\to k)\in E.

4.4  Problem-solving bindings

The bindings Σ\Sigma make the team’s problem-solving structure explicit so that system views have something to inspect other than chat. Σ\Sigma declares: roles with responsibilities, a perspective and capabilities; representations—user sources and per-member append-only structured notes—with explicit readers and writers; work units with phase, actors, inputs, outputs and dependencies; version-specific handoffs from a producer to a consumer with an acknowledgement requirement; an expertise directory that records which members are assigned which topics, with the declared basis (“user-editable role emphasis, not verified expertise”); a temporal reference ordering the phases with a deadline wave; and affordances, the capability-conditioned action opportunities a member actually has (publish to a note; acknowledge a handoff). teamknitt init generates these bindings mechanically from purpose, member count, topology and sharing; the user edits them directly rather than regenerating. The default task-team design runs four phases—independent proposals, task adoption, parallel episodes and evidence review—and asks members to frame, connect, develop and review while preserving alternatives before converging.

4.5  Execution loop

Figure 3 shows one dependency wave. A member observes only its permitted inputs, representations and affordances, externalizes a bounded contribution with input provenance, and the controller validates all publications of the wave before committing immutable versions. Consumers encounter permitted versions in a later wave and acknowledge specific handoffs. The record distinguishes available, exposed, published and acknowledged, and keeps report freshness and missingness explicit. Delegation, decision tools, retries and corrections draw on the same request cap. The default contribution is bounded text; code or external actions require an explicitly permitted tool and its receipt, and the design instructs members not to pretend otherwise. Completion means contributions were produced and retained for review in trials/ID/deliverable.md; it is not a verified outcome.

5  Observing the work: two groups of views

The same configuration and record can be observed through two groups of views (Table 4). The grouping follows explanatory locus (Section 2.1). It is an orientation for the observer, not a partition of science or a pair of execution presets, and switching groups is presentation-only.

Non-system views

The collaborative-intelligence view is member-focused and behavioural. teamknitt ships original synthetic alone/baseline/challenged probes informed by the Collaborative Intelligence benchmark [44]; they run in a separate workspace, use alone performance for eligibility, leave incomplete cells unknown rather than zero, and can be attached to a task view only as separate-context evidence. Ordinary task telemetry does not evaluate the eight capabilities. The shared-models view compares explicit member reports: reported plans, conformity to a declared reference, freshness and perceived alignment. These are compositional proxies by construction and are labelled as such; similarity is not accuracy [27].

System views

The distributed problem-solving view inspects the bindings of Section 4.4 together with recorded transformations and handoffs, in the spirit of [19, 29]. The transactive-memory view inspects the configured expertise directory as a differentiated pattern [42, 23], and says so when the directory is merely configured rather than demonstrated. The interactive-cognition view inspects exposure and acknowledgement receipts [6]; a configured route is never substituted for a missing observation. The dynamics view exposes optional descriptive observations.

Optional process observations

When enabled, four descriptive dimensions are derived from the record: local–global, contribution and receipt activity alongside handoff-state continuity; perturbation, explicit disturbance windows with baseline sufficiency, overlap, maintenance or return, first attainment and right censoring; coupling, directed artifact-exposure and provenance counts; and cross-level, member, artifact and coordination records together. Three further dimensions—attractors, synchronization and fractals—are listed so that their absence is explicit: no estimator is implemented, and dependency waves are neither evenly spaced nor uniform in content. Variability in contribution activity is reported, not read as flexibility or resilience.

6  Intervention

Human-team research addresses intervention at several levels: staffing and role design, task design, procedures and enabling conditions [14, 15]; cross-training and perturbation training [10]; and team training in general [37]. teamknitt offers one explicit mechanism for each timing (Table 5) and refuses to collapse them: a changed input, a changed process, a report of alignment and an improved outcome are different claims.

Queue semantics

Requests are prepared from the command line (the browser desk prepares commands and reads receipts; it cannot write the queue or start execution). A request without --apply is a preview. An applied request binds one run and one configuration identity and is read by the runtime before it begins a dependency wave, outside any publication transaction. The record then separates five claims that are easy to conflate:

queued≠applied at boundary≠context assembled≠understood≠improved.\textit{queued}\;\neq\;\textit{applied at boundary}\;\neq\;\textit{context assembled}\;\neq\;\textit{understood}\;\neq\;\textit{improved}.

A context-assembly event is metadata about constructing a member’s frame; it is not proof that a provider received the text or that a model used it. A request arriving after the last useful boundary is retained as not applied. Receipts carry recipients, timestamps, hashes, boundary waves and assembly counts, never message bodies. The queue is bounded (256 requests per run, 64 pending) and is a private file queue, not a multi-user or cryptographic authorization system.

Planned disturbances

A disturbance is scheduled before a run, with an explicit kind, target, wave and duration that must fit the configured system. It changes the configuration identity of a future run and never a historical record. The perturbation observation then reports baseline sufficiency, the disturbed window, whether a continuity measure was maintained or returned, first attainment and censoring. It reports no recovery score and infers no causal effect; the comparison condition, independent outcome evidence and analysis are the user’s.

7  Reference implementation

teamknitt 0.9.0 is a Python (≥\geq3.11) package with one console command and its own runtime, teamknitt.engine, which owns scheduling, provider and decision adapters, persistence, structural planning, schemas and resources [33]. It imports no upstream package and delegates to no other CLI. The core modules comprise roughly 7,300 lines; the offline test suite contains 21 modules and about 350 tests, and setup, planning, viewing, drafting, demonstration, diagram rendering and packaging make no provider calls. Table 6 separates implemented components from limits.

Offline demonstration

teamknitt demo runs deterministic “connected” and “fragmented” fixtures through the full configure–publish–observe path without a model, so that routes, barriers, receipts and views can be inspected before any budget is spent. Fixtures are software behaviour, not model evidence or a solution to the user’s task. Live execution requires an explicit provider, a private key, a reviewed plan and run --live --approve-requests N, where NN must equal the resolved request cap.

Observability

A local, read-only viewer and the offline snapshot show the resolved team, routes, bindings, grouped views, heartbeat and recorded completion. Live activity, stale metadata and recorded completion are visually distinct. Nothing in the browser applies a configuration, changes a budget or starts a model.

8  Research agenda: hypotheses and protocol

teamknitt is useful only if organizational and intervention claims about LLM-agent teams become testable. The hypotheses below are possibilities, not expectations; several are phrased so that either outcome would be informative about whether human-team regularities transfer.

  1. H1.

    Topology is inert without sharing. Under none, differences between presets in the diversity of retained alternatives vanish; they appear only at intermediate or above. (A manipulation check on P2–P3.)

  2. H2.

    Hubs converge faster, not better. At matched NN, WW and budget, hub_and_spoke retains fewer distinct alternatives at review than ring or grid, without a higher share of contributions judged useful by the user.

  3. H3.

    Direction limits relay. directed_chain preserves more of the first-wave alternatives than chain at equal exposure budget, because reciprocal routes allow content to return and recombine.

  4. H4.

    Redundancy and disturbance. After an actor_unavailable disturbance, handoff continuity returns sooner in topologies with alternative routes (ring, grid, wheel) than in chain or hub_and_spoke; whether variability in contribution activity before the disturbance predicts return, as the dynamical view of human teams suggests [11], is an open question.

  5. H5.

    Timing of feedback. Private feedback assembled before a transition phase (task adoption, evidence review) changes subsequent contributions more than feedback assembled during an action phase (parallel episodes), consistent with the temporal taxonomy of [26].

  6. H6.

    Member measures do not predict system records. A member’s separately measured teammate profile [44] predicts its in-team acknowledgement and relay behaviour only weakly once topology and sharing are controlled. A strong prediction would favour non-system explanation; a weak one would favour system explanation.

  7. H7.

    Same-model homogeneity. When all members use one model, topology differences shrink as sharing increases; heterogeneous model assignment widens them.

  8. H8.

    Fractality of communication output. Following [31, 13], the series of communication output exchanged between members (per-wave contribution and acknowledgement volume, inter-contribution intervals, and turnover in lexical content across versions) exhibits long-range correlation, and teams whose series show a scaling exponent in the persistent range (0.5<α<10.5<\alpha<1 under detrended fluctuation analysis) and a positive but bounded maximal Lyapunov exponent for discussion density receive higher user-judged usefulness and retain more distinct alternatives than teams whose series are closer to white noise or to rigid periodicity. Scaling that reflects only the scheduler’s wave structure must be ruled out with surrogate series and with the none baseline, where no inter-member communication occurs.

  9. H9.

    Cross-model fractality. When members run on different models, the output of each model carries its own scaling signature, and the degree to which those signatures align after exchange (relative to runs where the same models never see each other’s output) is associated with team performance; the sign of that association is left open, since alignment may indicate productive coupling or premature convergence.

Protocol

I propose a factorial design over topology (a selected subset of the fourteen presets), sharing profile (five) and member count (for example N∈{3,6,9}N\in\{3,6,9\}), with purpose, brief, model, request cap, read budget WW and review criteria held fixed, and custom with empty links as the isolated baseline. Each cell is replicated with fresh contexts. Outcomes are operational and human-reviewed: the number of distinct alternatives retained at review; the share of contributions the user judges useful against declared criteria; relay distance of first-wave content; acknowledgement rate and latency; handoff continuity around disturbances; and realized cost including corrections and delegation. Analysis is descriptive with frequentist count and interval estimates declared before review. teamknitt’s records—configuration identities, exposure logs, receipts and assembly events—are designed to supply these quantities directly. H8 and H9 need longer runs than the other hypotheses: scaling estimates require series of at least a few hundred points, so these studies would use goal-oriented missions with many waves, or many short runs of the same configuration whose per-wave series are analysed as an ensemble, with DFA and Lyapunov estimates compared against phase-randomized and shuffled surrogates [31]. The communication series themselves would be derived offline from the exported event store; no estimator runs inside the product.

Threats to validity

Four are immediate. Personas on one model may differ in label more than in behaviour; the mechanisms must be measured, not assumed. Field-based sharing filters cannot guarantee semantic isolation, so leakage is an outcome to quantify rather than a property to assume. Provider nondeterminism and silent model changes require replication and recorded model identities. Finally, human review of usefulness is itself a measurement with reliability that must be checked.

9  Limitations

The main limitation is the boundary of the paper: no empirical comparison of topologies, sharing profiles or interventions is reported. teamknitt supplies the apparatus, not evidence that any configuration is better. The grouped views are explanatory orientations applied to operational scaffolds; they do not measure the psychological constructs whose names they borrow, and the implementation says so at each view. The dynamical observations are descriptive, and the estimators used in the author’s earlier work [31]—detrended fluctuation analysis and Lyapunov exponents—are not applied inside the product, because wave-level records from a single run are short and unevenly spaced; H8 and H9 therefore depend on an offline analysis pipeline and on longer or pooled runs that do not yet exist. The teammate probes are original synthetic protocols informed by the Collaborative Intelligence benchmark, not the benchmark itself. Intervention receipts record assembly, not understanding; feedback effects are not estimated. The runtime defaults to bounded text work; code and external actions require explicitly permitted tools. Finally, the software is distributed under a source-available noncommercial and research licence rather than an OSI open-source licence: general noncommercial use is free, but research use outside qualifying academic institutions, and any commercial use, require separate written permission.

10  Conclusion

Every LLM-agent team has a topology, an information policy and a stance on human intervention, even when the framework hides them. teamknitt makes those three choices explicit and user-owned, and offers human-team theory as a lens for observing what happens rather than as a source of borrowed conclusions. The user chooses who is connected to whom and what may travel; observes the work through member-centred or interaction-centred views that never alter it; and intervenes through mechanisms whose scope, timing and receipts are recorded. Configuration identities, exposure logs and the chain from queued to improved then make it possible to ask, for agent teams, the questions that human-team research has been asking for decades: where does a team’s success or failure live, how does a team-level property arise, and when does intervening help? Whether the answers for LLM agents resemble the answers for people is an empirical question. teamknitt is intended to provide the apparatus for asking it.
